items.note: General description of the Bhūmija śikhara: four spines with chaitya-dormers on the central rathas and quadrants filled with miniature shrine-models in rows.
Style found favour with the Paramāras of Malwa; author states it originated in Malwa in the 10th century, attested at Amareshwara, Onkar Mandhata.

claim.value: originated in Malwa, 10th century (Amareshwara, Onkar Mandhata)

items.note: Udaipur (District Vidisha) temple of Nilakantheshwara or Udayeshwara after its royal author Udayaditya, grandest Paramara specimen, begun 1059, completed 1080; stellate plan, sapta-ratha sanctum, vestibule, hall with three porches.

Temple surrounded by 7 subsidiary shrines on an extensive platform-terrace with stepped entrance flanked by Shaiva dvarapalas; shikhara with 7 vertical and 5 horizontal rows of miniature shikharas per quadrant; sculptured medallions in chaitya-dormers.
Apsaras on the porch balustrades noted for grace and expression; monument remarkable for ornamentation, shikhara design and organic unity.

Un temples share plan and shikhara design with the Udayeshwara but are simpler; Chamunda, Nataraja and Shiva Tripurari in cardinal niches; an inscription of Udayaditya in Chaubara Dera No. 1 shows contemporaneity with the Udayeshwara.
Amareshwara securely dated 1063; Jamli later than Udayeshwara by about a decade; Nemawar's shikhara is loftier with nine rows but lacks the grace and proportion of the Udayeshwara.
Menal temple appears contemporary with the Udayeshwara; Ramgarh Shiva Temple about half a century later with similar plan and shikhara design.
Summary: the Bhumija style originated in Malwa, patronised by the Paramara rulers, with wide vogue in adjoining regions.

claim.value: originated in Malwa under Paramara patronage
